clue.text: "I write fiction because it's a way of making statements I can" (Tom Stoppard)

definitions.text: "I write fiction because it's a way of making statements I can" (Tom Stoppard)

parts.words: "I write fiction because it's a way of making statements I can" (Tom Stoppard)
parts.note: a quotation with its last word missing: the playwright says fiction lets him say things he can later refuse to own as his

explanation.surface: Tom Stoppard explains why he writes fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: To deny that something is yours is the missing verb; fiction lets a writer voice views and then deny them as his own.

clue.text: Called "dog", Macbeth thought, along with shough and water-rug

definitions.text: Called "dog", Macbeth thought, along with shough and water-rug

parts.words: Called "dog", Macbeth thought, along with shough and water-rug
parts.note: Macbeth lists breeds 'clept all by the name of dogs': shoughs, water-rugs and a half-wolf cross

explanation.surface: Macbeth's speech cataloguing breeds that all go by the name of dog.
explanation.walkthrough: In Macbeth III.i the king tells the murderers that hounds, greyhounds, mongrels, spaniels, curs, shoughs, water-rugs and demi-wolves are all called dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's word for a cross between a dog and a wolf, named in Macbeth's list of breeds.

clue.text: They give support, like Melvyn Bragg's inheritance and Mary Wesley's fiddle

definitions.meaning: assistants to a duellist or boxer stand by and back their principal

definitions.text: like Melvyn Bragg's inheritance and Mary Wesley's fiddle
definitions.meaning: Bragg wrote The Second Inheritance and Wesley wrote Second Fiddle, both titles opening with the same ordinal

explanation.surface: Two British novelists' book titles alongside helpers who lend support.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporters at a duel or boxing match bear this name, and both novel titles begin with the ordinal after first.

clue.text: Earl Rivers in a hanger over French town

parts.note: a hanger is a wood on the side of a steep hill
ville is French for town

explanation.surface: A nobleman stationed in a hillside wood above a town in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' places the wood before the town in this down clue. Anthony Woodville, 2nd Earl Rivers, was Edward IV's brother-in-law, executed by Richard III.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Woodville held the title Earl Rivers in the fifteenth century, so the title names the man by his surname.

clue.text: Ronsard, and six other stars, belonged to the first of the French ones

definitions.text: Ronsard, and six other stars, belonged to the first of the French ones

parts.words: Ronsard, and six other stars, belonged to the first of the French ones
parts.note: Ronsard led a group of seven poets named after the seven-star cluster in Taurus; seven luminaries make one such group

explanation.surface: The French poet Ronsard and six fellow luminaries formed a famous literary circle.
explanation.walkthrough: The French Renaissance circle of seven poets led by Ronsard and du Bellay took its name from the star cluster, as an Alexandrian group of poets had earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: The Seven Sisters cluster of stars gave its name to groups of seven poets, Ronsard's being the first French one.

clue.text: Yeatsian version of Veronese subject

parts.note: Yeats wrote a sonnet on the myth of Zeus as a bird seducing a mortal queen, a scene Veronese also painted

explanation.surface: An Irish poet treating a theme from an Italian painter's canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeats's sonnet of 1924 and Veronese's painting share the myth of Zeus, disguised as a bird, ravishing a Spartan queen.

clue.text: Frank but manipulative friend of the scion of Hermiston

definitions.text: Frank but manipulative friend of the scion of Hermiston

parts.words: Frank but manipulative friend of the scion of Hermiston
parts.note: in Stevenson's Weir of Hermiston, the scheming friend of young Archie Weir has the first name Frank

explanation.surface: An outspoken yet scheming companion of a laird's heir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like an adjective (candid) clashing with 'manipulative', but it is the character's first name in Stevenson's unfinished novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Surname of Frank, the meddling friend of Archie Weir in Robert Louis Stevenson's unfinished novel Weir of Hermiston.

clue.text: US novelist becomes ill in dole mix-up

indicators.note: the word ill is set inside the jumbled letters of dole
a mix-up muddles the order, so the letters of dole are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An American writer falls sick amid a muddle over unemployment benefit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becomes' is a link word. In Britain 'the dole' is everyday slang for unemployment benefit, so the surface reads as a muddle at the benefits office.
explanation.definitionFit: Don DeLillo is the American author of White Noise and Underworld.

clue.text: Seed of opening phrase in children's story

definitions.meaning: a small oily grain scattered on bread rolls
Ali Baba's password for the robbers' cave is 'open' followed by this word

explanation.surface: A grain and the magic words that open a cave in a tale for children.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a plant whose small seeds top bread and the word in Ali Baba's command that opens the thieves' cave.

clue.text: Confused Chandler sitcom reminiscent of Trollope work

indicators.note: confused means jumbled, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A muddled TV comedy by Chandler that recalls a Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reminiscent of' is a link. CHANDLER SITCOM has fourteen letters, matching the two words of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope's 1860 novel set in Ireland during the famine bears this title.

clue.text: The literary world got a rough shaking from him in 1891

definitions.text: The literary world got a rough shaking from him in 1891

parts.words: The literary world got a rough shaking from him in 1891
parts.note: a Scottish fantasy writer published a boys' novel titled A Rough Shaking in 1891

explanation.surface: An author who jolted the literary establishment in 1891.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a rough shaking' reads as a jolt to the world of letters, but it is the title of George MacDonald's 1891 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: George MacDonald, the Scottish author of Phantastes, published the novel A Rough Shaking in 1891.

clue.text: O'Neill artillery captain, reminiscent of white and blue flowers

definitions.meaning: an army officer in a Eugene O'Neill play bears this surname
flowers are things that flow, rivers: the White and Blue branches meet at Khartoum

explanation.surface: A soldier in an O'Neill drama recalling blossoms of white and blue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flowers' means rivers here, things that flow; the White and Blue Niles join at Khartoum. 'reminiscent of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural of the African river whose White and Blue branches merge, and the surname of an artillery officer in O'Neill.

clue.text: Container, but not quite butt, such as Clarence encountered

definitions.text: Container, but not quite butt, such as Clarence encountered

parts.words: Container, but not quite butt, such as Clarence encountered
parts.note: Shakespeare's Duke of Clarence was drowned in a butt of malmsey, a cask for a sweet fortified drink

explanation.surface: A cask, not exactly a butt, like the one Clarence met his end in.
explanation.walkthrough: In Richard III, Clarence is murdered and drowned in a butt of malmsey; a butt is a large barrel, close to but not quite a vintner's tank.
explanation.definitionFit: A large tank or cask for fermenting or storing the drink, akin to the barrel of malmsey in which Clarence drowned.

clue.text: Title Faulkner used twice

parts.note: Faulkner's 1936 novel repeats one biblical name in its title, followed by an exclamation mark

explanation.surface: A heading William Faulkner reused.
explanation.walkthrough: It seems to mean two books with one title, but the title itself is the name said twice: Absalom, Absalom!
explanation.definitionFit: The rebellious son of King David whose name Faulkner doubled in his novel's title.

clue.text: "Do not recruiting sergeants drum through the streets and collect ragged —s enough?" (Carlyle)

definitions.text: "Do not recruiting sergeants drum through the streets and collect ragged —s enough?" (Carlyle)

parts.words: "Do not recruiting sergeants drum through the streets and collect ragged —s enough?" (Carlyle)
parts.note: Carlyle's sentence has a gap for an archaic word meaning a worthless wastrel

explanation.surface: Carlyle mocks army recruiters gathering up ragged good-for-nothings.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for a scoundrel or ne'er-do-well, the sort of ragged idler recruiting sergeants rounded up.

clue.text: Lyly's man in the moon

parts.note: John Lyly's court comedy is subtitled The Man in the Moon, its hero a shepherd loved by the moon goddess

explanation.surface: The Elizabethan dramatist Lyly's lunar figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The shepherd beloved of the moon goddess Cynthia, hero of Lyly's play subtitled The Man in the Moon.

clue.text: Colour of satellite described by Collins

parts.note: the moon is Earth's natural satellite
stone is a pale greyish beige colour

explanation.surface: The hue of a moon as depicted by a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' joins the pieces: the colour of the satellite becomes a moon-stone. Wilkie Collins wrote The Moonstone, an early detective novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilkie Collins's 1868 detective novel centres on the theft of a yellow gem of this kind.

clue.text: Part of joint including New York's poet

indicators.note: including means the joint part holds the New York piece inside it

parts.note: a tenon is the projecting part of a mortise-and-tenon joint
NY is New York, with its possessive S

explanation.surface: A section of a joint containing a New Yorker's verse.
explanation.walkthrough: A mortise-and-tenon joint is a woodworking joint; the surface makes 'poet' sound like a New Yorker's verse rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was Victoria's Poet Laureate.

clue.text: There, mid revisions of Victorian novelist

indicators.note: revisions rework a text, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Edits to a manuscript, there in the middle, by a writer of Victoria's era.
explanation.walkthrough: THERE MID gives exactly the letters of George Meredith's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: George Meredith wrote The Egoist and Diana of the Crossways in Queen Victoria's reign.

clue.text: Discreetly concealed effusions of Mark Antony's faithful servitor?

definitions.text: Discreetly concealed effusions of Mark Antony's faithful servitor?

parts.words: Discreetly concealed effusions of Mark Antony's faithful servitor?
parts.note: Antony's loyal servant in Shakespeare is named after the god of love, so his writings would be amorous

explanation.surface: Hidden outpourings from Mark Antony's loyal attendant.
explanation.walkthrough: In Antony and Cleopatra Antony's servant is Eros; the effusions of Eros would be love writing, the kind kept discreetly out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Sexually explicit literature, the sort kept hidden, playfully credited to Eros, the god of love and Antony's servant.

clue.text: Speechify in 27 (at zero speed)

parts.note: zero looks like the letter O
rate means speed, as in a rate of knots

explanation.surface: Making speeches in churches, without moving at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 is ORATORIES; speechifying is what one does in oratory. 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver a pompous speech, the art practised in oratory.

clue.text: Describing one of Coleridge's "organic harps diversely framed"

definitions.text: Describing one of Coleridge's "organic harps diversely framed"

parts.words: Describing one of Coleridge's "organic harps diversely framed"
parts.note: Coleridge's poem about a wind-played harp imagines all nature as such instruments

explanation.surface: A word describing one of Coleridge's living harps.
explanation.definitionFit: Of the wind god, so a harp sounded by the wind, as in Coleridge's poem The Eolian Harp.

clue.text: Debar dictionaries including definition of heroic verse

indicators.note: the run of words includes the answer inside them, spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Banning dictionaries that contain a definition of epic poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from deBAR into DICtionaries. 'definition' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to bards, the poets who sang heroic and epic deeds.

clue.text: Of boy who sneezed at Cher Antoine: He only does it to —, because he knows it teases?

definitions.text: Of boy who sneezed at Cher Antoine: He only does it to —, because he knows it teases?

parts.words: Of boy who sneezed at Cher Antoine: He only does it to —, because he knows it teases?
parts.note: the Duchess's lullaby in Alice says the sneezing boy does it to annoy; the dramatist of Cher Antoine has a name sounding much like that verb

explanation.surface: Lewis Carroll's sneezing boy transplanted to a French play.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap in Carroll's line is 'annoy'; Jean Anouilh, author of Cher Antoine, has a name pronounced close to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Anouilh, the French dramatist who wrote Cher Antoine, whose surname sounds like the missing word in Carroll's verse.

clue.text: They gave Decianus the sack at Colchester

definitions.text: They gave Decianus the sack at Colchester

parts.words: They gave Decianus the sack at Colchester
parts.note: Boudica's tribe sacked Colchester and drove out the Roman procurator Catus Decianus

explanation.surface: Someone fired a man called Decianus at Colchester.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gave the sack' looks like dismissal; they sacked Colchester (Camulodunum) and put the procurator Catus Decianus to flight in AD 60.
explanation.definitionFit: The East Anglian tribe led by Boudica that rose against Rome and sacked Colchester.

clue.text: By and by surround donkey for an infantry officer

indicators.note: surround means the time phrase is put around the animal

parts.note: by and by means soon
an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: Encircle a donkey shortly, on behalf of an army officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for an' is a link. 'By and by' is an old-fashioned phrase for 'before long'.
explanation.definitionFit: Siegfried Sassoon served as a junior officer with the Royal Welch Fusiliers on the Western Front and wrote war poetry.

clue.text: What a critic cannot do, although knowing the way, Tynan thought

definitions.text: What a critic cannot do, although knowing the way, Tynan thought

parts.words: What a critic cannot do, although knowing the way, Tynan thought
parts.note: Kenneth Tynan said a critic is a man who knows the way but cannot take the car

explanation.surface: Tynan's view of what critics are unable to do.
explanation.definitionFit: Tynan's quip: a critic knows the route but cannot operate the car.

clue.text: So a rioter reformed in churches of St Philip Neri

indicators.note: reformed means formed anew, so the letters of the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A troublemaker reforms and joins a religious order's churches.
explanation.walkthrough: SO A RIOTER has nine letters, the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Neri founded the Congregation of the Oratory, whose priests serve in houses and chapels bearing that name.

clue.text: She attracted crotchety eccentrics

parts.note: a literary heroine of this name drew odd admirers, the sentence played as if about a musical instrument's crotchets

explanation.surface: A woman who drew in cranky oddballs.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns, as Sylvander, wrote love letters to Agnes McLehose under this name; 'crotchety' hints at music notes and the clarinet.
explanation.definitionFit: The pen name of Agnes McLehose, Robert Burns's correspondent, a heroine who drew in odd admirers.

clue.text: Sir Frederick, some strong believer (no-nonsense type) in Rob Roy

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: A firm believer, a no-nonsense type, in Scott's novel Rob Roy.
explanation.walkthrough: The name runs from believER into NONsense. Sir Frederick Vernon is Diana Vernon's father in Scott's Rob Roy. 'type) in Rob Roy' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Frederick Vernon, Jacobite father of the heroine Diana in Walter Scott's Rob Roy, carries this surname.
